old_body: Alexander 'Sandy' Douglas was a Cambridge PhD student when he made a noughts-and-crosses program for EDSAC, usually dated to 1952. The player entered moves with a rotary telephone dial. A small cathode-ray display showed the board, and the player could choose whether to move first or let the machine begin.

The setting shaped the audience. EDSAC was a research computer, so this was not a product that people could buy and take home. Few people outside Cambridge encountered the program. Its significance lies partly in that small scale: a laboratory machine could become something a person played against, with an input device, a visible position and a response to each decision.

The surviving EDSAC simulator and its documentation make that interaction approachable today. They also remind us to distinguish an original program from a later reconstruction. OXO is an important early graphical computer game; its position among other beginnings depends on whether we mean a stored program, an electronic display, moving images or public access.
old_headings: A telephone dial meets a computer
A game inside a research laboratory
What a reconstruction can show us

old_body: The Intellivision (a portmanteau of "intelligent television") is a home video game console released by Mattel Electronics. It distinguished itself from competitors with more realistic sports and strategic games. By 1981, Mattel Electronics had close to 20% of the domestic video game market, selling more than 3.75 million consoles and 20 million cartridges through 1983. At its peak, Mattel Electronics had about 1,800 employees in several countries, including 110 videogame developers. In 1984, Mattel sold its video game assets to a former Mattel Electronics executive and investors, eventually becoming INTV Corporation. Game development ran from 1978 to 1990, when the Intellivision was discontinued.

Its controllers asked players to learn a different vocabulary. A disc registered sixteen directions, while a twelve-key pad and side buttons offered more inputs than a simple paddle. Sports helped make the argument for the hardware. Mattel's advertising compared its baseball with Atari's, while programmers worked around a less visible problem: the display hardware could draw only eight moving objects at once.

The solution depended on decisions about what needed to move and what could temporarily become part of the background. A busy playing field was an effect constructed within limits, not an unlimited canvas. The Blue Sky Rangers' retrospective describes these techniques and the people behind them. Looking at the original console alongside that account brings the commercial promise and the programming work into the same frame: a machine sold through the picture, and games made through careful compromises.
